articles.title: How MSU students aided the nation's 'blue tsunami'
articles.description: It's been a week since Michigan voters elected the nation's first Muslim to serve in the U.S. Senate and flipped the state's 7th Congressional District blue. Central to Michigan's "blue tsunami" were Michigan State University students. "To look around and see states that are completely red being flipped was an absolute dream," MSUCollege Democrats President Aastha Singh said. The 2026 midterm elections were defined by the Democratic Party's attempts to gain control of the U.S. Congress after losing the senate and the executive branch in the 2024 presidential election. The contest fell amid internal strife within the party, which remained divided throughout the midterm cycle over backing progressive challengers instead of Establishment candidates. As ballots were counted, the Democratic Party flipped seven Republican-held Senate seats and two dozen House districts, regaining control of both legislative branches in a historic run of progressive victories. The Republican Party failed to flip a single Democratic-held seat in the nation. In the state of Michigan, the governor's office, the state Senate and the state House of Representatives are now also under the control of the Michigan Democratic Party. "(This is) the outcome of people and communities organizing and getting people to understand that work can be done - that we can have a more progressive government that will actually benefit people," Singh said. Math secondary education senior Izzy Cyncewicz has volunteered for U.S. Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed's campaign since May, and helped to start the Spartans for Abdul organization, where she serves as secretary. She said the nationwide progressive victories inspire within her a hope in democracy that she hasn't felt in a long time. "I can't even put into words how I am feeling - I feel like I've been walking on cloud nine," Cyncewicz said. The work of Cyncewicz and other students played a decisive role in the outcome of Michigan's 7th Congressional District race - more than anywhere else in the nation, according to a recent Tufts University study. The decisiveness of the student vote was seen very clearly on election night, Cyncewicz said. A late-hour surge as the Ingham County vote was tallied propelled progressive challenger William Lawrence ahead of incumbent U.S. Rep. Tom Barrett, R-Charlotte, in the race for Michigan's 7th Congressional District. Lawrence beat Barrett by 37 points in Ingham County, a larger margin than any other county in Michigan's 7th Congressional District. El-Sayed beat Republican opponent Mike Rogers by 39 points in Ingham County, the third largest margin of victory for El-Sayed in the state. On-campus voting rose over 110% compared to the 2022 midterm elections, an independent data analysis from The State News found. On-campus registration for the 2026 midterms also rose significantly compared to 2022, according to Ingham County results. Students registered to vote in on-campus precincts went from 4,140 people in 2022 to 7,450 in 2026. MSU Dems, MSU Sunrise, Spartans for Abdul and Spartans for Will all mobilized towards one goal. They phone banked, dorm stormed, door knocked and canvassed for months, doing everything they could to steer students to the polls. Janna Carlson, a campus organizer and field lead for Spartans for Will and MSU Sunrise, expressed gratitude for student volunteers, especially in determining the outcome of Michigan's 7th Congressional District. "Money is what billionaires want us to think wins elections, but they are so wrong," Carlson said. "It's the people who win the elections." Michigan's 7th congressional District race set a U.S. House record for ad spending this election cycle with candidates and political action committees spending more than $66 million on political advertisements. "We beat impossible odds … by the power of the people, students and community," Carlson said. "It's the students who knocked on thousands of doors on campus, it's the community who knocked on over 300,000 doors." The state of the U.S. economy under the Trump administration greatly aided the progressive wave and the blue turn of the youth vote, Singh said, his promises of economic prosperity now falling on deaf ears. "When things begin to affect you personally, you start to look around and realize this is not a system that benefits you," she said.
